title: The specification says the class names are generated and change on every build, and neither is true
foundBy: repository owner (host), asking: "did we hard-code numbers? cs-component-tree-92?"

evidence.verified: `components/Tree.md` no longer says the class names are generated or that they change on every build, and gives the true reason to prefer the documented hooks instead. `scripts/check-integrity.mjs` now fails rather than warns on a stale name, and its comment no longer offers the two grounds that had gone: a search of `src/` and `preview/src/` finds no name composed by interpolation, and no script generates one. Both failure directions were provoked and observed. A class defined in `page.css` and referenced nowhere reports `.cs-component-page-99 is defined but referenced by no component source`, and a class referenced in `Page.tsx` and defined nowhere reports the reverse, each naming its file and line. Both restores were byte-identical and the run returned to PASS. `npm run ci` exits 0 at 91b303d.

details:
`components/Tree.md` tells a consumer to prefer the documented `data-part` hooks over "the generated class names, which change on every build". They are not generated, and they do not change.

`cs-component-tree-92` is a literal string in `src/components/Tree.tsx` at line 952, with nine rules under that selector in `src/styles/components/tree.css`. It reaches the published build verbatim, and two consecutive `npm run build` runs produced a byte-identical `dist/components/Tree.js`.

Nothing in this repository generates these names. The only scripts that name `cs-component-` are `check-integrity.mjs` and `check-consumer-dom-contract.mjs`, and both only read them. The numbering is a fossil of a one-time conversion away from utility classes, which `--tw-space-y-reverse` in `preview/src/preview.css` still shows.

The advice is right and its reason is false, which is the pairing that costs a reader later. Someone who checks the claim finds the names stable and starts depending on one. Nothing renumbers it for them, and nothing warns when a hand edit does.

`scripts/check-integrity.mjs` carries the same claim in the comment above its class hygiene check, where it is also the stated reason that check only warns rather than failing.

notes.text:
A correction to this record's own details, and an addition that makes it actionable.

The details call the numbering a fossil of a one-time conversion away from utility classes. The history does not support that. `src/styles/components/tree.css` arrives with these names in `d8462fb`, the initial implementation, so no conversion happened in this repository. A `--tw-space-y-reverse` property in `preview/src/preview.css` and a commit message calling two variables Tailwind-era are circumstantial. Whatever produced the names predates the first commit, and this record should not have asserted otherwise.

The addition is that both reasons `scripts/check-integrity.mjs` gives for warning rather than failing are now false. Nothing generates the names, and no name is composed dynamically: every `cs-component-` occurrence under `src/` and `preview/src/` is a complete literal, with interpolation only ever appended after a finished name. So that check could fail rather than warn, which would make a stale name an error instead of a line nobody reads.

One piece of evidence for the maintenance cost, from the session that filed this. Allocating a new name meant scripting a search for the highest number in use, 505, and taking 506. Removing this component's content wrapper left `cs-component-page-5` deleted while `-6` stayed in use, so the sequence has a hole. Nothing objects to either, because nothing is watching.

Closed on the false statements rather than on the naming scheme. Renaming the classes to something a reader can interpret was considered and not done. `scripts/check-consumer-dom-contract.mjs` exists to audit a consumer's repository for references to exactly these names, so the project expects consumers to reach for them whatever the DOM contract says. A rename would break those consumers, and the case for it is maintainer comfort.

If that rename is ever wanted, the way in is one component at a time as each is touched, after running `npm run check:consumer-dom` to see who would break. Not as one change.
